source.title: Compute Optimal Inference and Provable Amortisation Gap in Sparse Autoencoders

page_placements.theme: Encoder inference and optimization affect feature recovery

record.tranche_reason: Tests superposition-related decoder geometry in synthetic sparse representations and evaluates learned features on GPT-2, using methods and measures different from the original toy-model study.
record.gate_note: The paper reports synthetic sparse-code inference and recovery results, but those measure inference performance rather than the overlap geometry or capacity account in the claim, so they are not rows here. GPT-2 feature interpretability scores and synthetic decoder-geometry results are included. Background claims and results cited from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper on the SAE amortisation gap. It takes superposition as a premise, builds synthetic data that is superposed by construction, and compares encoders (SAE, MLP, sparse coding, SAE+ITO, LCA) on sparse-code recovery and GPT-2 auto-interpretability. None of its results measure whether a network stores features in superposition, or test the capacity account, polysemanticity, SAE feature canonicality or feature dimensionality. The Appendix E decoder Gram matrices describe the geometry of learned dictionaries, not a model's own representations. Their off-diagonal values near 1.0 indicate near-duplicate dictionary columns, a recovery failure, rather than the nearly orthogonal overlap V1 describes; the authors' 'superposition' label there is loose. The GPT-2 F1 scores compare the authors' encoders with each other and include no neuron baseline.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors prove an amortisation gap for L-NL SAE encoders, show sparse coding (and sometimes MLPs) recover synthetic sparse codes better, and find MLP-encoder features more interpretable on GPT-2. Their Appendix E 'superposition' reading of SAE and MLP decoders is a side observation about learned dictionaries, not a claim about how models represent features.
record.recipe_differences: The paper compares SAE, MLP, sparse coding, and inference-time optimisation rather than reproducing the original toy-model method; it also evaluates learned decoder geometry and GPT-2 feature interpretability.
record.method_sensitivity: Decoder superposition diminishes with vector normalisation; decoder geometry differs across SAE, MLP, and sparse coding.

fits_no_version.finding: A theorem shows that a linear-nonlinear SAE encoder cannot exactly recover all K-sparse codes even where compressed sensing guarantees they can be recovered. On synthetic data, SAE latent MCC trails sparse coding by about 10%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents are imperfect (amortisation-limited) estimates of the true sparse features, which bears on the fidelity of dictionary features (near V5) but does not test completeness, stability or canonicality.

fits_no_version.finding: On GPT-2 L9, dictionaries with an MLP encoder score higher on auto-interpretability (median F1 0.83) than SAE (0.63) or LCA (0.61) dictionaries of the same size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The interpretability of dictionary features depends on the encoder architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: Learned SAE and MLP dictionaries on synthetic superposed data contain near-duplicate columns (off-diagonal Gram entries near 1.0), while sparse-coding dictionaries are closer to orthogonal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The geometry of a dictionary-learning method's recovered features depends on its inference method.

record.problems: Decoder-geometry evidence is presented largely as qualitative heatmaps without numerical estimates. GPT-2 interpretability is evaluated on 500 sampled features using an automated GPT-4o procedure, not ground-truth feature recovery, and covers only Layer 9.
record.rows_left_out: Synthetic sparse-inference and dictionary-learning MCC results, including the varying-K experiments in Sections 4 and Appendix D, are left out because they measure recovery performance rather than the claim's superposition geometry, capacity account, or LLM feature distribution. Background citations are also excluded.
record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T2 is overstated. The paper uses superposition as background and as its synthetic data model. Its core results concern the inference quality of SAEs versus alternative encoders, so it falls under T4. Labels for V1 and V4 were removed because no row measures the claim's construct in a network's own representations. Synthetic MCC results were correctly left out as recovery performance.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test a sparsity-dependent transition or regular geometry across sparsity levels; varying K is used for sparse-inference performance, not decoder geometry. Does not establish how feature importance changes the geometry.
Does not test whether polysemanticity results from capacity competition, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while others share.
Does not test whether polysemanticity arises for reasons other than capacity pressure.
The GPT-2 evaluation tests interpretability of learned features, not whether those features are complete ground-truth features or how widely they are distributed across the model's neurons.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Uses dictionary vectors to represent learned features but does not compare one-dimensional features with multi-dimensional alternatives.

rows.subject: SAE
rows.size_stated: GPT-2 Small; activation dimension 768; dictionary size 16,896
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated feature interpretability using GPT-4o-generated explanations and held-out activation examples.
rows.measure: F1 score for predicting feature-activating examples from an explanation
rows.uncertainty: The paper reports a Kruskal-Wallis test across methods, H = 1856.33, p < 0.001; no SAE-specific error bar is stated.
rows.note: This is indirect evidence of interpretability of learned SAE features, not a comparison with ground-truth features.
rows.check: The subject is an SAE trained on GPT-2 activations, not a toy network. The value is median F1 0.63 per the figure (text: 'around 0.6'). The row is part of the study's comparison of its own encoders. Without a neuron baseline it cannot show whether features are spread across neurons.

source_check.problem: Method comparator; should not be a claim-result row. Its interpretability score cannot determine any listed claim version.

relation.reason: Uses the superposition framework to motivate feature recovery and evaluates its own encoding methods, without independently testing a listed claim version.

tranche.reason: Assumes superposed representations and compares sparse-inference methods. Synthetic superposition is constructed; GPT-2 results measure dictionary interpretability. Appendix E examines learned decoder geometry without establishing a listed claim version.

source_check.notes: Figure 7 explicitly gives 0.63, 0.83 and 0.61; prose confirms 0.83 and describes the others as around 0.6. Prose and caption specify 500 features per method, while plot annotations show N=2500 without explanation.
